newsitem.title: UK: UK house prices up at fastest rate since '88 - RICS.
newsitem.headline: UK house prices up at fastest rate since '88 - RICS.

text.p: British house prices are climbing at the fastest rate since 1988, seemingly immune to the uncertainties of a looming general election, or fears of interest rate rises, a survey out on Tuesday said.

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors said over 10 percent of chartered surveyors who contributed to the survey said house prices have risen by more than five percent over the three months to the end of March.
Aside from 1988, when the housing market was spiralling out of control, this is the first time that has happened since the survey began 20 years ago.

"The housing market seems to be immune to the election," said RICS housing market spokesman Ian Perry. "Even the widely predicted interest rate rise in early May and possible phasing out of MIRAS (mortgage interest relief) is unlikely to have any appreciable effect."

Labour's Gordon Brown, widely tipped to become Chancellor of the Exchequer after May 1 elections, with the Labour Party still streets ahead in the polls, is expected to quickly raise interest rates to establish his anti-inflationary credentials.
Despite hefty price rises in some areas, the RICS said the housing recovery remained patchy, with the market being led by buoyant conditions in London, the South East and the Midlands.
In the capital, a net balance of 90 percent of chartered surveyors saw an increase in prices as did 87 percent of those in the South East and 67 percent in the West Midlands.

In contrast, only 34 percent of those in the North reported rising prices, along with a mere 33 percent in Yorkshire and Humberside. East Anglia lagged worst, with only 15 percent of chartered surveyors there seeing higher house prices.
The pick-up in prices cannot be seen as a 1980s-style boom, the RICS said, because the number of transactions, at 1.3 million per year, remained low. In 1988, that rate was 2.2 million.
But Perry said a 20 billion stg flood of windfall payments from building societies converting into banks, which will land over the next few months, will continue to fuel a housing recovery.
"That combined with a marked rise in the number of valuations being carried out, means that we can look forward to more property coming onto the market and more choice for homebuyers," he said.
